cases.question: Why does merge sort's running time stay the same no matter how the input is ordered?
cases.answer: Merge sort always splits the array in half, so the recursion is about log n levels deep whatever the data looks like. At every level it merges all n items once, which is linear work, so the total is O(n log n) in the best, average and worst case. It never looks at the order to decide how to split, unlike quicksort with its pivot.

cases.question: Why is insertion sort fast on an array that is already nearly sorted?
cases.answer: Insertion sort slides each new item left past the larger items until it reaches its place. If the array is nearly sorted, every item is only a few places from where it belongs, so it only slides a little. On a fully sorted array each item is compared once with its left neighbour and stays put, so the whole thing is O(n) instead of the O(n^2) worst case.

cases.question: How can quicksort end up taking quadratic time, and how can that be avoided?
cases.answer: If quicksort picks a bad pivot it gets really slow, so you should pick a better pivot.

cases.question: Compare merge sort and quicksort in terms of extra memory and stability.
cases.answer: Merge sort needs a helper array, so it uses O(n) extra memory, while quicksort partitions in place and doesn't need one.

cases.question: How much work does selection sort do on an array that is already sorted, and why?
cases.answer: Selection sort notices that the array is already in order after the first pass and stops early, so on sorted input it only takes O(n) time, which is why it is the best choice for nearly sorted data.

cases.question: What is a collision in a hash table, and how does separate chaining deal with it?
cases.answer: A collision is when two different keys hash to the same bucket. With separate chaining each bucket keeps a short list of the entries that landed there, and a lookup goes to the bucket and walks that list to find the right key.

cases.question: Why do hash tables resize when the load factor gets high?
cases.answer: The load factor is entries divided by buckets. As it grows, more keys share buckets, so collisions become more common and lookups slow down. Past a threshold like 0.75 the table allocates a bigger array and inserts every entry again, which brings the load factor back down and keeps lookups close to constant time.

cases.question: Explain the two ways the notes describe for handling collisions.
cases.answer: One way is separate chaining, where each bucket holds a list of the entries that hash there and a lookup walks the list.

cases.question: Why does a poor hash function make a hash table slow?
cases.answer: A poor hash function doesn't spread the keys out well, so the table gets slower.

cases.question: How does a hash table find the value for a key?
cases.answer: It keeps all the keys sorted in one array and uses binary search to find the key, which is why lookups take O(log n) time.
